t5_AI_SAP.title: Enhancing SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce Quality ...
t5_AI_SAP.content:
- **Exact title:** Enhancing SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce Quality Assurance & Quality Control through AI-Driven Test Automation Frameworks for Regulatory Compliance
- **Author(s):** Not stated on the page.
- **Publisher/journal:** *International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering*
- **Publication year:** 2025
- **Claims about AI/generative AI in SAP programs:** The article introduces an AI-based test automation framework for SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce implementations that uses machine learning algorithms and natural language processing for intelligent test case generation, predictive risk evaluation, self-healing test scripts, and automated compliance checking. The page does not mention SAP Joule, Cloud ALM, functional specifications, cutover, or hypercare.
t5_AI_SAP.description: Both enterprise resource planning and customer relationship management systems are under increasing pressure to ensure that they remain compliant with their regulations and provide efficient quality assurance processes. The outdated testing models are not capable of keeping up with the dynamics of current enterprise platforms, especially those that are closely regulated, such as the healthcare and medical device manufacturing industries. In this article, an AI-based test automation framework is introduced to support quality assurance and quality control processes during the implementation of SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce by means of machine learning algorithms and natural language processing. It has an intelligent test case generation, predictive risk evaluation, self-healing test scripts, and an automated compliance checking framework. Case studies of implementations show that efficiency of testing, detection of defects, and coverage of regulatory compliance have been greatly enhanced in the financial services and healthcare sectors, as well as within the medical device manufacturing settings. The framework considers major technical issues such as data quality management, the complexity of system integration, and regulatory validation requirements with the help of modular architecture and standard protocols of interfaces.
t5_AI_SAP.author: Vijay Kumar Kola
t5_AI_SAP.hostname: International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering

| Relevant content | The paper documents a systematic approach to transferring project knowledge from external and internal sources to where it should be applied. It identifies the individual, project, and organisational levels, and states that an incentive system, a data repository, and a reporting system are needed for an integrated knowledge-transfer solution; the PMO is described as the architect and facilitator of knowledge transfers between these levels. |
| Figures stated | The page states that studies covered **more than 400 companies**, of which **272 reported having PMOs**; among those 272 PMOs, **8%** did not support knowledge-management processes, **46%** supported some, **41%** supported most, and **4%** supported all. | Knowledge loss | The page states that knowledge transfer is difficult when knowledge is held by individuals, who may trade it informally through the “grapevine effect,” leaving people outside the specific social network unable to gain from others’ knowledge. It also warns that if most staff leave a relatively small organisation, ongoing projects can be seriously jeopardised. |
t7_memory.description: Knowledge transfer is crucial to a company's operations. This paper proposes that project management offices (PMOs) should play an important role in managing knowledge transfer. An emphasis on data repository, incentives, and reporting systems as key elements leads to a discussion of the routes knowledge transfer takes at the individual, project, and organizational levels.

- **Author(s):** National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
- **Publisher/journal/standards body:** National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
- **Publication year:** 2023

- **Human oversight / human-in-the-loop requirements and findings:**
  - The Framework states that processes for human oversight must be defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies. It also requires organizations to define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems.
  - Human oversight may be necessary when an AI system cannot detect or correct errors; practical AI safety approaches include real-time monitoring and the ability to shut down, modify, or introduce human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality. It also notes that human-AI configurations can range from fully autonomous to fully manual, and that some systems may not require human oversight while others specifically require it.

t8_HITL.title: Article 14: Human Oversight | EU Artificial Intelligence Act
t8_HITL.content:
- **Title:** Article 14: Human Oversight
- **Author(s):** Not stated
- **Publisher/journal/standards body:** Not stated
- **Publication year:** year not stated
- **Requirements regarding human oversight:** High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed with appropriate human-machine interface tools so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use. Human oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights and must enable oversight personnel to understand the system’s capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, detect anomalies and dysfunctions, account for automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, disregard or override outputs, and intervene or stop the system safely.
- **Additional human-in-the-loop requirement:** For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, deployers generally may not take action or decisions based on the system’s identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent, trained, and authorised natural persons; this requirement does not apply where Union or national law considers it disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum purposes.

t8_HITL.title: Human-in-the-Loop Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review of Concepts, Methods, and Applications
t8_HITL.content:
- **Title:** Human-in-the-Loop Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review of Concepts, Methods, and Applications
- **Authors:** Konstantinos Lazaros; Aristidis G. Vrahatis; Sotiris Kotsiantis
- **Publisher/journal/standards body:** MDPI; *Entropy*
- **Publication year:** 2026
- **What it requires/finds regarding human oversight / human-in-the-loop in AI systems:** The review specifies HITL AI as a design paradigm in which human input has operational impact on AI model development, deployment, supervision, or governance. It finds that effective oversight requires appropriate authority, information, time, expertise, and the ability to evaluate and override AI decisions; high-stakes applications generally require tighter human control, while oversight must also address scalability, cognitive load, trust calibration, fairness, accountability, and adversarial manipulation.
t8_HITL.description: The integration of human judgment into artificial intelligence (AI) systems has emerged as a key research direction, particularly for high-stakes applications where full automation remains insufficient. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) AI represents a field that combines machine learning capabilities with human oversight, feedback, and decision-making at various stages of the AI pipeline. This survey provides a systematic review of HITL approaches, covering theoretical foundations, technical methods, ethical considerations, and domain-specific applications. We propose a unified taxonomy that categorizes HITL systems based on loop placement, interaction granularity, and temporal characteristics. This review synthesizes findings from healthcare, autonomous systems, cybersecurity, and other high-risk domains where human oversight is essential. We also examine the challenges of scalability, cognitive load, and trust calibration that affect the practical deployment of HITL systems. The final section outlines open research directions and introduces a framework for designing effective human–AI collaborative systems.
t8_HITL.author: Konstantinos Lazaros; Aristidis G Vrahatis; Sotiris Kotsiantis; Lazaros; Konstantinos; Vrahatis; Aristidis G; Kotsiantis; Sotiris

The study finds that having a human banker in the loop of AI-based financial advisory, with the banker given the final say over the advice, does not compromise advice quality. Bank customers are more likely to align their final investment decisions with human–AI collaborative advice than with pure AI advice, particularly for riskier investments; the increased persuasive efficacy is attributed largely to human involvement serving as a peripheral cue that enhances the advice’s affective appeal rather than to perceived complementarities in human and AI capabilities.
